title: Squeeze and rebuild
objectives: Build an autoencoder with a bottleneck, and read its reconstruction error.

screens.title: Squeeze to one number
screens.prose: Each dot is one day of two oil stocks' returns, with the average day moved to the origin. We **squeeze** each day to one number, where it lands on the line, then **rebuild** it as that point on the line. Drag the handle to turn the line.
screens.question: Turn the line until the total squared rebuild distance is as small as you can make it.

hints.text: Watch the dashed lines: each is one day's rebuild miss.
The line should run along the cloud, from bottom left to top right.
The best line has a total of 1.38; aim for it.

feedback.correct: Along the cloud the total falls to 1.38, from 16.08 with the line flat.
feedback.generic: Not yet. Keep turning until the dashed misses are as short as they get.

byKey.axis: A flat line keeps only stock A. The total is 16.08: stock B's moves are all lost.
byKey.steep: That line is too steep: the days spread more across it than along it.

explain.text: The best line runs along the cloud. Each day keeps one number, yet the total squared miss is only 1.38, against 45.12 for rebuilding every day as the average day.

screens.title: Encoder and decoder
screens.prose: What you just did is an **autoencoder**. An **encoder** turns a day $\mathbf{x}$ into a shorter **code** $z = \mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{u}$, and a **decoder** rebuilds $\hat{\mathbf{x}} = z\,\mathbf{u}$. Take the unit direction $\mathbf{u} = (0.8, 0.6)$ and the day $\mathbf{x} = (2.0, 1.4)$.
screens.question: Fill in the code and the rebuilt day.

hints.text: The code is a dot product with $\mathbf{u}$.
$z = 2.44$; multiply $\mathbf{u}$ by it.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Dot $\mathbf{x}$ with $\mathbf{u}$, then scale $\mathbf{u}$ by the result.

byKey.sum: You added the two returns. Weight them by $\mathbf{u}$: $0.8 \times 2.0 + 0.6 \times 1.4$.

explain.text: The encoder keeps $z = 1.6 + 0.84 = 2.44$. The decoder puts the day back on the line at $(1.952, 1.464)$, a miss of about 0.08.

screens.title: Three days, one error
screens.prose: The **reconstruction error** is the mean, over days, of the squared distance from each day to its rebuild. Keep $\mathbf{u} = (0.8, 0.6)$. The days are $(2, 1)$, $(-1, -1)$ and $(0.5, -1)$; their codes are $2.2$, $-1.4$ and $-0.2$.
screens.question: What is the reconstruction error of these three days? Give a decimal.

hints.text: A squared distance is the squared length minus the squared code, when $\mathbf{u}$ has length 1.
The three are 0.16, 0.04 and 1.21; take their mean.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Square each day's miss, then average over the three days.

byKey.sum: 1.41 is the total. The error is the mean over the three days.
byKey.dist: You averaged the distances. The error averages their squares.

explain.text: By Pythagoras each miss squared is the squared length minus the squared code: 0.16, 0.04 and 1.21. The day $(0.5, -1)$ lies across the line and costs most; the mean is 0.47.

screens.title: How big a bottleneck?
screens.prose: Now five stocks, 2,000 days. The **bottleneck** is the number of codes each day keeps. The bars show the reconstruction error of the best linear autoencoder of each size; with 0 codes every day is rebuilt as the average day.
screens.question: With 2 codes, what share of the no-code error is left? Give a percentage to the nearest whole number.

hints.text: Divide the error with 2 codes by the error with none.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the 2-code bar by the 0-code bar.

byKey.kept: That is the share removed. The question asks what is left.
byKey.one: That is the share left with 1 code. Read the 2-code bar.

explain.text: Two codes leave $1.01/5.04 \approx 20\%$ of the error. Each extra code helps less, and 5 codes for 5 stocks leave nothing.

screens.title: Train one
screens.prose: We trained a linear autoencoder with 2 codes on the five stocks: $\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{x}\mathbf{W}_{\text{enc}}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{z}\mathbf{W}_{\text{dec}}$, small random starts, Adam (`nn-train` L1) with step size 0.05, for 300 steps. The curve is its reconstruction error.
screens.question: Where does the training error settle? Give a decimal to 2 places.

hints.text: Read the right-hand end of the curve.
It meets the dashed line from the bars.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Read where the curve flattens.

byKey.one: That is the 1-code bar. This model keeps 2 codes.
byKey.start: That is where training starts, from small random weights.

explain.text: Training finds the 2-code bar, 1.01, without being told it. The next lesson shows why the best linear autoencoder lands exactly there.

screens.title: Zero error, nothing learned
screens.prose: A colleague trains a linear autoencoder with 5 codes on the same five stocks. It rebuilds every day exactly: reconstruction error 0. They call it the best representation of the data.
screens.question: What is wrong with their claim?

options.text: Five codes for five numbers can simply copy each day, so zero error shows that nothing was squeezed
Zero error means it has memorised the noise, so it will fail on new days
options.why: Copying works on any day, new ones too. Nothing was learned at all, which is a different fault from memorising.

options.text: It needs more training before its codes become useful
options.why: More training cannot help: the model can already copy, and copying is all its loss asks for.

options.text: Its error on held-out days would be large, which exposes it
options.why: A copy rebuilds held-out days exactly as well. The held-out error is 0 too.

hints.text: How many numbers does each day have, and how many does the code keep?
With as many codes as inputs, the identity map is allowed.

feedback.correct: Right. A code as wide as the input can be the input itself.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what a 5-number code can do with a 5-number day.

byKey.noise: You read zero error as overfitting. Copying is worse: it learns nothing, and still scores 0 on new days.
byKey.held: You expected held-out days to expose it. A copy rebuilds them perfectly too.

explain.text: Low error is only meaningful when the code is smaller than the input. Judge a representation by what it keeps at a given bottleneck, not by the error alone.

screens.title: As wide as the input
screens.prose: Two stocks, two codes, no squeezing at all. Here $\hat{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{x}\mathbf{W}_{\text{enc}}\mathbf{W}_{\text{dec}}$, so the error is 0 exactly when $\mathbf{W}_{\text{enc}}\mathbf{W}_{\text{dec}} = \mathbf{I}$.
screens.question: Which pairs $(\mathbf{W}_{\text{enc}}, \mathbf{W}_{\text{dec}})$ rebuild every day exactly? Select all that apply.

options.text: $(\mathbf{I}, \mathbf{I})$
$(\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{R}^\top)$
$(\mathbf{S}, \mathbf{S}^{-1})$
$(\mathbf{S}, \mathbf{S})$
options.why: $\mathbf{S}\mathbf{S}$ stretches the first column by 4. That is not the identity.

options.text: $(\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{R})$
options.why: $\mathbf{R}\mathbf{R}$ turns twice. Undoing a turn needs $\mathbf{R}^\top$.

hints.text: Multiply each pair and compare with $\mathbf{I}$.
$\mathbf{R}\mathbf{R}^\top = \mathbf{I}$ for a rotation.

feedback.correct: Right. Any invertible encoder with its inverse as decoder copies every day.
feedback.generic: Not quite. A pair works when the decoder undoes the encoder.

explain.text: Any invertible $\mathbf{W}_{\text{enc}}$ with $\mathbf{W}_{\text{dec}} = \mathbf{W}_{\text{enc}}^{-1}$ gives zero error. So a full-width code is not even unique: the codes mean nothing in particular.

screens.title: The autoencoder
screens.prose: An autoencoder has an encoder $\mathbf{z} = f(\mathbf{x})$ to a code smaller than the input and a decoder $\hat{\mathbf{x}} = g(\mathbf{z})$. Training lowers $$L = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \lVert \mathbf{x}_i - g(f(\mathbf{x}_i)) \rVert^2.$$ The linear case is $f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}\mathbf{W}_{\text{enc}}$, $g(\mathbf{z}) = \mathbf{z}\mathbf{W}_{\text{dec}}$.
screens.question: What does this loss need besides the days themselves?

options.text: Nothing: the target is the input, so no labels are needed
A label for each day, such as up or down
options.why: The loss compares each day with its own rebuild. No label appears in it.

options.text: The principal components, to set the code
options.why: Training finds the code from the loss alone. The components come into the next lesson as a check, not an input.

feedback.correct: Right. The day is its own target.

explain.text: The loss compares each $\mathbf{x}_i$ with its own rebuild, so the data supply both input and target. This is why autoencoders learn from unlabelled data.

import numpy as np
from autograd import Tensor
from nt_ops_l1 import adam_step


def train_autoencoder(X, k, steps, lr, seed):
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    X = X - X.mean(axis=0)              # centre each column
    n, d = X.shape
    g = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    W_enc = Tensor(0.1 * g.standard_normal((d, k)))
    W_dec = Tensor(0.1 * g.standard_normal((k, d)))
    params = [W_enc, W_dec]
    m = [np.zeros_like(p.data) for p in params]
    v = [np.zeros_like(p.data) for p in params]
    for t in range(1, steps + 1):
        for p in params:
            p.zero_grad()
        D = X @ W_enc @ W_dec - X
        loss = (D ** 2).sum() / n
        loss.backward()
        new, m, v = adam_step([p.data for p in params], [p.grad for p in params], m, v, t, lr)
        for p, q in zip(params, new):
            p.data = q
    return W_enc.data, W_dec.data

import numpy as np
from autograd import Tensor
from nt_ops_l1 import adam_step


def train_autoencoder(X, k, steps, lr, seed):
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    X = X - X.mean(axis=0)              # centre each column
    n, d = X.shape
    g = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    W_enc = Tensor(0.1 * g.standard_normal((d, k)))
    W_dec = Tensor(0.1 * g.standard_normal((k, d)))
    params = [W_enc, W_dec]
    m = [np.zeros_like(p.data) for p in params]
    v = [np.zeros_like(p.data) for p in params]
    for t in range(1, steps + 1):
        for p in params:
            p.zero_grad()
        D = X @ W_enc @ W_enc.T - X
        loss = (D ** 2).sum() / n
        loss.backward()
        new, m, v = adam_step([p.data for p in params], [p.grad for p in params], m, v, t, lr)
        for p, q in zip(params, new):
            p.data = q
    return W_enc.data, W_dec.data

screens.title: A panel in three numbers
screens.prose: A risk team keeps 500 days of returns on 30 stocks: 15,000 numbers. A linear autoencoder with 3 codes stores 500 days of codes plus a $3 \times 30$ decoder, 1,590 numbers, and keeps 61% of the variance on our seeded panel.
screens.question: What do the 3 codes throw away?

options.text: Mostly each stock's own moves, the part no shared driver explains
The market move, since it is the same for every stock
options.why: The market move is the largest shared driver. It is the first thing the code keeps.

options.text: The sector moves, which only a labelled model can find
options.why: The codes found the shared moves without labels. Sectors are among what they keep.

options.text: Nothing that matters, since the error is small
options.why: The rest of the variance is real: it is each stock's own news, which a hedge on one name needs.

hints.text: The first bars are the shared drivers.
What is left after the shared moves?

feedback.correct: Right. The codes keep the shared moves and drop each stock's own news.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask which moves are shared by many stocks.

byKey.market: You thought a common move is lost. It is the move most worth keeping.
byKey.nothing: You read a small error as no loss. A single stock's own news is exactly what is dropped.

explain.text: Three codes hold the market and the sectors, 61% of the variance. The rest is stock-specific news, which matters for anyone trading one name.

ideas: An autoencoder encodes each input to a shorter code and decodes it back; training lowers the mean squared rebuild distance, with no labels.
The bottleneck size sets the error: each extra code lowers it, by less each time, to 0 at full width.
Zero error at full width is empty: an invertible encoder and its inverse copy every input.

formula.name: Reconstruction error
formula.note: Sum the squares along each row, then average over rows.

summary.trap: Low reconstruction error is not a good representation when the code is as wide as the input: the model can copy.
